59.1: This hymn by Vasiṣṭha is mostly for the Maruts, the storm gods. It begins: whoever you gods protect and guide — Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Maruts and Aryaman — please give them shelter.
59.2: With the gods' kindness, the worshipper overcomes his troubles on a lucky day. The one who makes offerings sees his home and food increase.
59.3: Vasiṣṭha says he will not forget even the smallest of the Maruts. 'Come quickly, all of you, and drink the Soma we pressed today!' Every member of the team matters.
59.4: 'Your help in battle never hurts the one you bless. Let your kindness come to us again — come quickly, you who love to drink Soma.'
59.5: 'Come here to drink the Soma, you generous ones! These offerings are for you — don't go anywhere else!'
59.6: 'Sit on our sacred grass and kindly give us the wealth we wish for. Enjoy the sweet Soma with the call of Svāhā, friends of all.'
59.7: The Maruts arrive like swans with purple backs, flying down secretly. Their whole group gathers around the poet like happy heroes.
59.8: The poet asks the Maruts to stop anyone whose anger is hard to control and who might attack without warning — to tangle him in his own mischief.
59.9: 'O Maruts, enjoy this offering made for you, and help us, you who defeat enemies.'
59.10: 'You share in the household worship — come, Maruts, don't stay far away, so you can help us, generous ones.'
59.11: 'Here, self-strong Maruts, wise ones with skin bright like the sun — I offer this worship to you.'
59.12: The famous MAHĀMṚTYUÑJAYA MANTRA to Rudra, the 'three-eyed one': like a ripe cucumber that comes off its stem easily, may we be freed from death and fear, and not separated from what is everlasting. People chant it for health and courage.

86.1: Vasiṣṭha praises Varuṇa, who is so great that he pushed apart the wide heaven and earth, set the sky and stars moving and spread out the earth. Everything wise in the world comes from his greatness.
86.2: Vasiṣṭha talks to his own heart: 'How can Varuṇa and I be close again? Will he accept my gift without being angry? When will I see that he is kind to me?' He feels something has gone wrong.
86.3: He asks wise people what is wrong, and they all say the same thing: 'Varuṇa is angry with you.' Sometimes we need others to help us see our mistakes.
86.4: 'Varuṇa, what was my big mistake that you are upset with a friend who praises you? Tell me, and I will quickly come to you, cleaned of wrongdoing, and bow to you.'
86.5: 'Free us from mistakes our ancestors made and those we made ourselves. O King, set Vasiṣṭha free, the way a calf is untied from its rope.'
86.6: Vasiṣṭha explains honestly: we often go wrong not on purpose but because of temptation, carelessness, strong drink, gambling or anger. Even sleep does not keep us from all wrongdoing.
86.7: 'Like a faithful servant, may I serve the generous god, free from wrongdoing.' Varuṇa gives wisdom to the simple and leads the wise to good things.
86.8: 'O Varuṇa, may this praise reach your heart. May all go well with us when we rest and when we work. Protect us always, gods, with your blessings.' A beautiful prayer of saying sorry and starting fresh.

103.1: The FROG SONG! All year the frogs lay quiet, like priests keeping a vow of silence. Now Parjanya, the rain god, has sent rain — and the frogs raise their voices!
103.2: The frogs lay in the dry pond like a dried-up leather bag. When the rain pours down, they all croak together, like cows mooing with their calves.
103.3: When the rains come to the thirsty frogs, one goes to another and greets him with happy croaks, like a child calling 'Papa!' to his father.
103.4: The frogs welcome each other, enjoying the water. The frog soaked by rain jumps forward, and the green one and the spotted one croak together.
103.5: One frog repeats what the other says, like a student repeating the teacher's words. This is how the Vedas themselves were learned — by repeating after the teacher!
103.6: One frog sounds like a cow, another bleats like a goat; one is green and one is spotted. They all have the same name, 'frog', yet each has its own voice. Different, but together!
103.7: Like priests sitting around a full vessel at a night-long Soma ceremony, the frogs gather around the pond to celebrate the first day of the rainy season.
103.8: The frogs are compared to priests who finish a year-long ceremony and raise their voices, and to priests sweating over hot pots who now come out. Everyone appears when the rain comes.
103.9: The frogs keep the order of the year set by the gods — they never miss the season. When the rains return, the frogs who were 'heated like pots' in summer are finally free.
103.10: Cow-voice, Goat-voice, Green and Spotted — the poet playfully says the frogs have given riches and long life. Their croaking means rain has come, and rain means food and life for everyone.
